'''weary<sup>2</sup>''' (wēr′i), ''n.'' [< *''weary''<sup>2</sup>, v., var. of ''wary''<sup>2</sup>, curse: see ''wary''<sup>2</sup>.] A curse: used now only in the phrases ''Weary fa’ you! Weary on you!'' and the like. ''Scott.'' [Scotch.]

'''weasand''' (wē′zand), ''n.'' [Also ''weazand'', and formerly ''wesand'', ''wezand'', also dial. ''wezzen'', ''wizen'', ''wizzen'', and ''wosen''; < ME. ''wesand'', ''wesande'', ''waysande'', ''wesaunt'', < AS. ''wǣsend'', also ''wāsend'' (> E. dial. ''wosen'') = OFries. ''wāsende'', ''wāsande'', weasand, windpipe, = OHG. ''weisunt'', MHG. ''weisant'' (E. Müller), weasand; cf. G. dial. (Bav.) ''waisel'', ''wasel'', ''wasling'', the gullet of ruminating animals. The word (AS. ''wāsend'') has the form of a present participle, and some have attempted to connect it with ''wheeze''; this involves the assumption that the rare AS. verb ''hwēsan'' (pret. ''hweós''), wheeze, = Icel. ''hvæsa'', hiss, = Dan. ''hvæse'', hiss, wheeze (not found in OHG., etc.), gave rise to a noun *''hwēsend'', varying to *''hwǣsend'', *''hwāsend'', meaning ‘the wheezing thing,’ that this name was applied to all windpipes (most of which never wheeze), and that subsequently the initial consonant in ''hw''- fell away, a phenomenon wholly unknown in other AS. words in ''hw''-, and not recognized even in mod. English except in dialectal use.] The windpipe; the pipe or tube through which air passes to and from the lungs in respiration; the trachea. See ''trachea''<sup>1</sup> and ''larynx.''
{{smaller block|Should I have named him? Nay, they should as soon have this ''weasand'' of mine.
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}
Had his ''wesand'' bene a little widder.
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., September.}}}}

'''weasel-cat''' (wē′zl-kat), ''n.'' The linsang, ''Prionodon gracilis.'' See cut under ''delundung.''

'''weasel-coot''' (wē′zl-köt), ''n.'' The so-called red-headed smew. {{smaller|This is the female or young male of ''Mergellus albellus'' (the adult male of which is figured under ''smew''). The implication of the term ''weasel'' appears to be the musteline or foxy color of the head. An old name of this or a similar merganser was ''Mergus mustelinus'', and one used by Sir T. Browne was ''Mustela variegata.'' The same adjective with the same meaning occurs in ''Turdus mustelinus'', the present name of the wood-thrush of the United States, and in several other specific designations of animals, as in ''Lepilemur mustelinus'', the weasel-lemur. Compare ''weaser.''}}

'''weasel-duck''' (wē′zl-duk), ''n.'' Same as ''weasel-coot.''

'''weasel-faced''' (wē′zl-fāst), ''a.'' Having a thin, sharp face like a weasel’s. ''Steele.''

'''weasel-fish''' (wē′zl-fish), ''n.'' The three-bearded rockling, or whistle-fish. See ''whistle-fish.''

'''weasel-lemur''' (wē′zl-lē″mėr), ''n.'' A small lemur, ''Lepilemur mustelinus.''

'''weaselling†''', ''n.'' [Also ''weazelling''; < ''weasel'' + ''ling''<sup>1</sup>.] A kind of rockling, probably the five-bearded, ''Motella mustela.''

'''weaselmonger†''' (wē′zl-mung″gėr), ''n.'' A rat-catcher; one who hunts rats, etc., with weasels.
{{smaller block|This ''weaselmonger'', who is no better than a cat in a house, or a ferret in a conygat [rabbit-burrow].
{{right|''Peele'', Speeches to Queen Elizabeth at Theobalds, ii.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wearisome|6861|}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|''Tiresome'' is more often used where one is acted upon; in strength it is the same as ''wearisome''. ''Tedious'' is stronger than ''wearisome'', and suggests the need of constant effort of the will to do or to endure; the weariness may be physical or mental: as, a ''tedious'' task; a ''tedious'' headache; ''tedious'' garrulity. ''Tedious'' suggests commonly that one is acted upon; ''irksome'' suggests that one acts or is called upon to act, and implies also a peculiar reluctance. In Shak., 2 Hen. VI., ii. 1. 56, is an example of the rarer use of ''irksome'' to express a wearied shrinking from being acted upon: “How ''irksome'' is this music to my heart!” See ''fatigue'', ''n.'', and ''tire''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.''}}

'''wearisomely''' (wēr′i-sum-li), ''adv.'' In a wearisome manner; tediously; so as to cause weariness.

{{smaller block|Pope’s epigrammatic cast of thought led him to spend his skill on bringing to a nicer adjustment the balance of the couplet, in which he succeeded only too ''wearisomely'' well.
{{right|''Lowell'', New Princeton Rev., I. 156.}}}}

'''wearisomeness''' (wēr′i-sum-nes), ''n.'' The quality or state of being wearisome; tiresomeness; tediousness: as, the ''wearisomeness'' of waiting long and anxiously.

{{smaller block|That the ''wearisomnesse'' of the Sea may bee refreshed in this pleasing part of the Countrie.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|Continual plodding and ''wearisomeness.''
{{right|''Milton'', Tetrachordon.}}}}
{{smaller block|It would be difficult to realize the ''wearisomeness'' which reigned in the Conclave during so protracted a period.
{{right|''J. H. Shorthouse'', John Inglesant, xxx.}}}}

'''wear-plate''' (wãr′plāt), ''n.'' Same as ''wear-iron.''

'''weary'''<sup>1</sup> (wēr′i), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wery'', ''weri'', < AS. ''wērig'' = OS. ''wōrig'' (in comp.), weary, = OHG. ''wōrag'', ''wuarag'', drunken. Cf. AS. ''wōrian'', wander, travel, roll, < *''wōr'', prob. a moor or wet place (> ME. ''wor'': “''wery'' so water in ''wore'',” ‘dull as water in pool’), in comp. ''wōr-hana'', a moorcock; cf. AS. ''wōs'', also ''wās'', mire, wet, ooze: see ''wase''<sup>2</sup>, ''woose'', ''ooze''.]   '''1.''' Tired; exhausted by toil or exertion; having the endurance or patience worn out by continuous striving.

{{smaller block|There nere is the place where that oure Lord rested him, whan he was ''wery'' for berynge of the Cros.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|Estern tewysday to Suza to Diner, and the I rest me; for I was ''were'', and my hors also, ffor the grett labor that I had the same mornyng in passing over the evyll and grevows mounte Senes.
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let us not be ''weary'' in well doing. {{right|Gal. vi. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|When they will they work, and sleep when they are ''weary''. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|I see you are ''weary'', and therefore I will presently wait on you to your chamber.
{{right|''Cotton'', in Walton’s Angler, ii. 235.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The stag-hounds, ''weary'' with the chase,
Lay stretched upon the rushy floor.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' Impatient of or discontented with the continuance of something painful, exacting, irksome, or distasteful, and willing to be done with it; having ceased to feel pleasure (in something).

{{smaller block|In the exercise and study of the mind they be never ''weary''. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Weary'' of the world, away she hies,
And yokes her silver doves.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1189.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I think she is ''weary'' of your tyranny,
And therefore gone. ''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, ii. 1.</poem>
He is ''weary'' of the old wooden houses, the mud and dust, the dead level of site and sentiment, the chill east wind, and the chillest of social atmospheres.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 11.}}}}
'''3.''' Causing fatigue; tiresome; irksome: as, a ''weary'' journey; a ''weary'' life.
{{smaller block|<poem>How ''weary'', stale, flat, and unprofitable
Seem to me all the uses of this world!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2. 133.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Their dusty palfreys and array
Showed they had marched a ''weary'' way.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, i}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Most ''weary'' seem’d the sea, ''weary'' the oar,
''Weary'' the wandering fields of barren foam.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lotos-Eaters.}}}}
'''4.''' Feeble; sickly; puny.   ''Forby; Jamieson.'' [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.] ='''Syn.''' {{smaller|Disgusted, wearisome. See ''weary''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''}}

'''weary'''<sup>1</sup> (wēr′i), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wearied'', ppr. ''wearying''.   [< ME. ''werien'', < AS. ''wērigean'', ''gewērigean'', weary, fatigue, < ''wērig'', weary: see ''weary''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make weary; reduce or exhaust the physical strength or endurance of; fatigue; tire: as, to ''weary'' one’s self with striving.
{{smaller block|The people shall ''weary'' themselves for very vanity.
{{right|Hab. ii. 13.}}}}
{{smaller block|They in the practice of their religion ''wearied'' chiefly their knees and hands, we especially our ears and tongues.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 81.}}}} '''2.''' To exhaust the endurance, patience, or resistance of, as by persistence or importunity.

431 {{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have even ''wearied'' heaven with prayers.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', ’Tis Pity, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Watchful I’ll guard thee, and with Midnight Pray’r
''Weary'' the Gods to keep thee in their Care.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Henry and Emma.}}}}

'''To weary out.''' (''a'') To exhaust or subdue by something fatiguing or irksome.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like an Egyptian Tyrant, some
Thou ''weariest out'' in building but a Tomb.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', The Mistress, Thraldom.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She surceased not, day nor night,
To storm me over-watch’d and ''wearied out.''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 405.}}}}
(''b'') To pass wearily. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The land of Italy:
There wil I waile, and ''weary out'' my dayes in wo.</poem>
{{right|''The Merchant’s Daughter'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 329).}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' ''Fatigue'', ''Jade'', etc. See ''tire''<sup>1</sup>.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To become weary, tired, or fatigued.
{{smaller block|<poem>She was nae ten miles frae the town,
When she began to ''weary.''</poem>
{{right|''Lizae Baillie'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 74).}}}}
'''2.''' To become impatient or surfeited, as with the continuance of something that is monotonous, irksome, or distasteful.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sing the simple passage o’er and o’er
For all an April morning, till the ear
''Wearies'' to hear it.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''3.''' To long; languish: with ''for'' before the object.
{{smaller block|The pair took home schoolboy meals in paper-bags, subsisting upon buns and canned meats, and ''wearying for'' the taste of a hot broiled steak. {{right|''The Century'', XXXVII. 775.}}}}
